metadata.name: TCP Three-Way Handshake
metadata.description: The sequence of SYN, SYN-ACK, and ACK packets exchanged between client and server to establish a TCP connection before any data is transmitted. A foundational coordination protocol of the internet, invisible to most participants but executed billions of times per day.
metadata.standpoint: Application developer; observing the protocol from the layer above (socket API), not from the network layer where packets live.

explicit.notes: Fully specified in RFC 793. No ambiguity about what constitutes the handshake.

institutional.notes: Governed by IETF RFCs — institutional in origin, though the institution is a consensus body.

immutable.notes: De facto immutable at the TCP level. TLS and QUIC layer on top rather than changing it.

monocultural.notes: Universal — same protocol regardless of who the client or server is.

exclusive.notes: Open to any device with a TCP/IP stack. Entry cost is technical, not social.

hierarchical.notes: Client initiates, server responds — slight asymmetry, but either party can close. Not strongly hierarchical.

determined.notes: Fully deterministic. Sequence numbers and state machine leave no room for interpretation.

macro.notes: Atomic interaction — a single connection setup, though it underlies systemic internet traffic.

obligatory.notes: Non-optional for TCP connections. Cannot skip or shortcut.

symmetric.notes: Client and server both send and receive, but the roles differ (initiator vs. listener).

voluntary.notes: Once software initiates a TCP connection, the handshake is not optional. The developer chose TCP; the protocol takes over.

agentic.notes: Fully automated. No human action or judgment during execution.

synchronous.notes: Sequential state transitions, though network delays mean it is not instantaneous.

legible.notes: Invisible to end users and most application developers. Legible only to network engineers with packet captures.

immediate.notes: Completes in milliseconds under normal conditions.

alive.notes: Extremely alive — executed billions of times per second globally.

smooth.notes: Frictionless when working; failure modes (retransmit, timeout) are invisible to most users.

pleasant.notes: Neither pleasant nor unpleasant — simply invisible infrastructure.

natural.notes: Feels natural because it is invisible, but is entirely artificial and historically contingent.

certain.notes: High reliability under normal conditions; uncertainty arises only in degraded network environments.

efficient.notes: Three-packet overhead is considered minimal for its reliability guarantees, though QUIC reduces this further.

exciting.notes: The least exciting protocol imaginable. Its virtue is its invisibility.

analysis.usefulness_notes: Useful for establishing baseline reference for what a 'hard' technical protocol looks like. The legibility gradient was the most revealing — it surfaces how protocol illegibility enables scale.

provenance.notes: Reference example entry for the Protocol Institute registry. Used as the template illustration in SKILL.md.
